column1: 00 HOW · How this deck differs from deck 1
column2: Deck 1 told you the question type on the front. This deck does NOT. | Sections 01-03 give you a bare question and make you CLASSIFY it yourself before solving. That classification step is the actual skill. | Sections 04+ cover the harder content tier: circles, trig, tangency, symbolic work.

column1: 00 HOW · Say the type out loud before you touch Desmos
column2: The single biggest difference between a 1300 and a 1450 is not computation, it is instant recognition. | Force yourself to name the type in words first: 'this is a mixed system with a parameter'. | If you cannot name it in ten seconds, flag it.

column1: 01 CLASSIFY · '2x + 3y = 12 and 4x + ky = 20 has no solution. What is k?'
column2: TYPE: system with a parameter, no-solution condition. | METHOD: no solution means PARALLEL, so slopes match but intercepts do not. Scale the first equation by 2 to get 4x + 6y = 24, so k = 6. | CHECK: intercepts differ (24 vs 20), so it is truly parallel and not identical.

column1: 01 CLASSIFY · 'f(x) = 2x^2 - 12x + 7. What is the minimum value of f?'
column2: TYPE: quadratic, vertex question, asking for the Y-value. | METHOD: vertex x = -b/(2a) = 12/4 = 3, then f(3) = 18 - 36 + 7 = -11. | DESMOS: graph it and click the minimum dot. | TRAP: 'minimum value' is the y-coordinate, not x = 3.

column1: 01 CLASSIFY · 'A total of 43 volunteers worked shifts of 3 or 5 hours for 173 hours total. How many worked 5-hour shifts?'
column2: TYPE: two-equation word problem (count plus value). | METHOD: x + y = 43 and 3x + 5y = 173. Desmos both, intersect: y = 22. | TRAP: read which shift length they asked about; x = 21 is the other coordinate and is offered.

column1: 01 CLASSIFY · 'The function g(x) = 250(0.88)^x models a value. By what percent does it decrease each step?'
column2: TYPE: exponential decay, interpret the base. | METHOD: 0.88 = 1 - 0.12, so it decreases 12 percent. | TRAP: 88 percent is the offered wrong answer. The base is what REMAINS; the decrease is 1 minus the base.

column1: 01 CLASSIFY · 'Line m passes through (2, 5) and is perpendicular to y = -4x + 1. What is its equation?'
column2: TYPE: linear equation from a point plus a perpendicularity condition. | METHOD: perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal of -4, which is 1/4. Then 5 = (1/4)(2) + b gives b = 4.5, so y = x/4 + 4.5. | TRAP: using -1/4 or +4 as the slope.

column1: 01 CLASSIFY · 'The mean of 6 numbers is 15. One number is removed and the mean becomes 13. What was removed?'
column2: TYPE: mean-change question. | METHOD: work in TOTALS. Old total 90, new total 5 x 13 = 65, so the removed value is 25. | This totals method handles every mean-change variant.

column1: 02 CLASSIFY · 'x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 6y + 18 = 0. What is the radius?'
column2: TYPE: circle in expanded form. | METHOD: DESMOS accepts it exactly as typed. Graph it and read the radius off the picture. | BY HAND: complete the square twice to get (x-5)^2 + (y+3)^2 = 16, radius 4. | Always try Desmos first here.

column1: 02 CLASSIFY · 'In the figure, a 12-foot ladder leans against a wall at 65 degrees to the ground. How high does it reach?'
column2: TYPE: right-triangle trig, need the side opposite the angle. | METHOD: sin(65) = height/12, so height = 12·sin(65) = about 10.9. | CRITICAL: set Desmos to DEGREES first, or you get a nonsense answer.

column1: 02 CLASSIFY · 'h(x) = (x-3)(x+5). For what value of x is h at its minimum?'
column2: TYPE: quadratic in factored form, vertex location. | SHORTCUT: the vertex sits exactly MIDWAY between the roots 3 and -5, so x = -1. | No expansion needed. This midpoint trick is worth memorizing.

column1: 02 CLASSIFY · 'A sphere and a cube have equal volume. The cube's edge is 6. What is the sphere's radius?'
column2: TYPE: work backward from a volume equation. | METHOD: cube volume 216, so (4/3)·pi·r^3 = 216. DESMOS: type (4/3)pi x^3 = 216 and click the intersection, r = about 3.72. | Beats taking a cube root by hand.

column1: 02 CLASSIFY · 'If 3^(2x) = 81, what is x?'
column2: TYPE: exponential equation with matching bases. | METHOD: 81 = 3^4, so 2x = 4 and x = 2. | DESMOS: graph y = 3^(2x) and y = 81, click the intersection. | TRAP: answering 4 by forgetting to divide by the 2.

column1: 02 CLASSIFY · 'Data set: 4, 7, 7, 9, 22. Which is larger, the mean or the median?'
column2: TYPE: center comparison with an outlier. | METHOD: median is 7; mean is 49/5 = 9.8. The mean is larger. | RULE: a high outlier drags the MEAN up but leaves the median alone. Knowing the rule answers it without computing.

column1: 03 CLASSIFY · 'The graph of y = f(x) is shifted 3 right and 2 down. Which defines the new function?'
column2: TYPE: function transformation. | METHOD: right 3 goes INSIDE as (x - 3); down 2 goes OUTSIDE as -2. Result: f(x - 3) - 2. | TRAP: horizontal shifts are backwards from how they read. Right means minus.

column1: 03 CLASSIFY · 'A line of best fit is y = 2.4x + 11. Interpret the 2.4.'
column2: TYPE: regression slope interpretation. | ANSWER: for each one-unit increase in x, the PREDICTED value of y increases by about 2.4. | TRAP: the correct choice almost always contains 'predicted' or 'on average'. Be wary of any choice that states it as a certainty.

column1: 03 CLASSIFY · 'A jar has 5 red, 8 blue, 7 green marbles. Given that a drawn marble is not green, what is P(red)?'
column2: TYPE: conditional probability. | METHOD: the condition RESTRICTS the denominator to non-green, which is 5 + 8 = 13. So P = 5/13. | TRAP: 5/20 uses the unrestricted total and is the offered error.

column1: 03 CLASSIFY · 'Triangle with sides 9, 12, and 15. What is its area?'
column2: TYPE: right triangle in disguise. | KEY: 9-12-15 is 3-4-5 scaled by 3, so it IS right-angled and the legs are 9 and 12. Area = (1/2)(9)(12) = 54. | Spotting the triple is the entire question.

column1: 03 CLASSIFY · 'Which is equivalent to (x^2 - 9)/(x + 3)?'
column2: TYPE: rational simplification via factoring. | METHOD: numerator is a difference of squares, (x-3)(x+3), so it cancels to x - 3. | TRAP: x = -3 must be excluded from the domain even though it cancels. If the question asks about domain, say so.

column1: 04 CIRCLES · Tangent line to a circle
column2: KEY FACT: the tangent is PERPENDICULAR to the radius at the point of contact. | METHOD: find the radius's slope from center to the point, then take the negative reciprocal. | Center (-4,-6) and point (-7,-7): radius slope = 1/3, so tangent slope = -3.

column1: 04 CIRCLES · Inscribed angle theorem
column2: An INSCRIBED angle (vertex on the circle) is HALF the central angle subtending the same arc. | So a central angle of 80 degrees gives an inscribed angle of 40. | An angle inscribed in a SEMICIRCLE is always 90 degrees.

column1: 04 CIRCLES · Two radii always make an isosceles triangle
column2: If O is the center and R, S are on the circle, then OR = OS, so triangle ORS is ISOSCELES. | The two base angles are equal: (180 - central angle)/2. | Central angle 88 gives base angles of 46 each. This unlocks most 'find the angle' circle questions.

column1: 04 CIRCLES · Arc length and sector area with radians
column2: With the angle in RADIANS: arc length = r·theta and sector area = (1/2)·r^2·theta. | With DEGREES: multiply the full circle by angle/360. | Check which unit the problem uses before choosing the formula.

column1: 04 CIRCLES · Equation of a circle through given points
column2: METHOD: if you know the center and one point on the circle, the radius is the DISTANCE between them. | Then write (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2 with r^2 left unsimplified if that matches the choices. | DESMOS: distance((h,k),(x,y)) computes it directly.

column1: 04 CIRCLES · Completing the square, both variables
column2: From x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0: halve D and E, square each, add both to the right side. | Center is (-D/2, -E/2) and r^2 = (D/2)^2 + (E/2)^2 - F. | Memorizing this formula beats doing the algebra twice under time pressure.

column1: 05 TRIG · The three ratios plus their reciprocals
column2: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. | Reciprocals: csc = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, cot = 1/tan. | The reciprocals appear rarely but do appear. Note that sec pairs with cos, which is the counterintuitive one.

column1: 05 TRIG · Exact values worth memorizing
column2: sin30 = 1/2, cos30 = sqrt(3)/2, tan30 = 1/sqrt(3). | sin45 = cos45 = sqrt(2)/2, tan45 = 1. | sin60 = sqrt(3)/2, cos60 = 1/2, tan60 = sqrt(3). | These come straight from the two special triangles.

column1: 05 TRIG · Complementary and supplementary identities
column2: sin(x) = cos(90 - x) and cos(x) = sin(90 - x). | sin(180 - x) = sin(x), while cos(180 - x) = -cos(x). | The first identity turns many hard-looking questions into one-second reads.

column1: 05 TRIG · Radian conversion and the key angles
column2: 180 degrees = pi radians. Degrees to radians: multiply by pi/180. Radians to degrees: multiply by 180/pi. | pi/6 = 30, pi/4 = 45, pi/3 = 60, pi/2 = 90, pi = 180, 2pi = 360. | Desmos will compute either, but only if the mode matches.

column1: 05 TRIG · Finding an angle from a ratio
column2: Use the inverse: if sin(x) = 0.6 then x = arcsin(0.6), typed as arcsin in Desmos. | MUST be in degree mode or you get radians. | TRAP: arcsin only returns angles between -90 and 90, so check whether the problem wants an obtuse angle instead.

column1: 05 TRIG · Angle of elevation versus depression
column2: ELEVATION is measured UP from the horizontal; DEPRESSION is measured DOWN from it. | They are equal alternate angles, so the same number works for both in most setups. | Draw the triangle and label the horizontal first; that prevents the usual mislabeling.

column1: 06 ADV-QUAD · Tangency means discriminant equals zero
column2: A line and a parabola meet at EXACTLY ONE point when the line is tangent. | METHOD: set them equal, collect into ax^2 + bx + c = 0, then force b^2 - 4ac = 0 and solve for the parameter. | DESMOS: slider the parameter and drag until the graphs just touch.

column1: 06 ADV-QUAD · Sum and product of roots
column2: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0: the roots SUM to -b/a and MULTIPLY to c/a. | Lets you answer 'what is the sum of the solutions' without solving at all. | Frequently faster than the quadratic formula and immune to sign errors.

column1: 06 ADV-QUAD · Building a quadratic from its roots
column2: If the roots are r and s, the quadratic is a(x - r)(x - s). | Given roots 4 and -2 with a leading coefficient of 3: 3(x-4)(x+2). | Expand only if the answer choices are in standard form.

column1: 06 ADV-QUAD · Number of real solutions from the graph
column2: Count where the curve CROSSES the x-axis: two crossings means two real solutions, a single touch means one, no crossing means none. | DESMOS: graph and count the x-intercept dots. | This replaces the discriminant entirely when you have a concrete equation.

column1: 06 ADV-QUAD · Symbolic quadratics with letters, no numbers
column2: SIGNAL: everything is a, b, c, k with no numerals. | STRATEGY: pick convenient SAFE NUMBERS for the letters, test the choices, and eliminate. Use values like 2 and 3, avoiding 0 and 1. | If two choices survive, pick a second set of numbers.

column1: 06 ADV-QUAD · Vertex form from standard form, fast
column2: x-coordinate of the vertex is -b/(2a). Plug it back in for k. Then the form is a(x - h)^2 + k. | No completing the square required. | DESMOS: click the vertex dot and read (h, k) straight off.

column1: 07 ADV-FUNC · Composite functions f(g(x))
column2: Work from the INSIDE OUT: compute g(x) first, then feed it into f. | DESMOS: define both on separate lines, then type f(g(2)). | TRAP: f(g(x)) is not g(f(x)); order changes the answer.

column1: 07 ADV-FUNC · Inverse functions
column2: METHOD: swap x and y, then solve for y. | The graph of the inverse is the original REFLECTED across the line y = x. | If f(3) = 7 then the inverse maps 7 back to 3, which answers many questions with no algebra.

column1: 07 ADV-FUNC · Reading a function's behavior off a table
column2: INCREASING means y rises as x rises. A constant DIFFERENCE between consecutive y-values means linear; a constant RATIO means exponential. | Compute both the differences and the ratios before deciding.

column1: 07 ADV-FUNC · Polynomial end behavior
column2: EVEN degree with positive lead: both ends up. Even degree with negative lead: both ends down. | ODD degree with positive lead: down on the left, up on the right. Odd with negative lead: the reverse. | Only the degree's parity and the lead coefficient's sign matter.

column1: 07 ADV-FUNC · Zeros, factors and multiplicity
column2: If (x - r) is a factor then r is a zero, and vice versa. | A zero of EVEN multiplicity TOUCHES the axis and turns back; ODD multiplicity CROSSES it. | A graph that bounces off the x-axis is telling you the factor is squared.

column1: 07 ADV-FUNC · Rational functions: asymptotes and holes
column2: A VERTICAL asymptote sits where the denominator is zero and the factor does NOT cancel. | If the factor cancels, you get a HOLE instead. | HORIZONTAL asymptote: compare degrees. Lower top means y = 0; equal degrees means the ratio of lead coefficients.

column1: 08 ADV-EQ · Extraneous solutions
column2: Squaring both sides or clearing a denominator can INVENT solutions that do not satisfy the original. | ALWAYS substitute your answers back into the ORIGINAL equation. | DESMOS sidesteps this: graph both sides and only genuine intersections appear.

column1: 08 ADV-EQ · Absolute value equations and inequalities
column2: abs(x) = k splits into x = k and x = -k. | abs(x) < k becomes the AND range -k < x < k. abs(x) > k becomes the OR pair x > k or x < -k. | DESMOS: graph y = abs(expression) and y = k, then read the intersections.

column1: 08 ADV-EQ · Systems of three equations
column2: METHOD: use one equation to eliminate a variable from the other two, reducing to a 2x2 system. | DESMOS is less helpful here since it graphs in 2D. | At a 1450 target this is uncommon; do not over-invest in it.

column1: 08 ADV-EQ · Exponential equations needing logs
column2: If the bases cannot be matched, take the log of both sides: x = log(k)/log(b). | DESMOS: just graph both sides and click the intersection. Much faster and no log rules to remember. | The SAT rarely requires true log manipulation.

column1: 08 ADV-EQ · Literal equations with fractions and multiple letters
column2: METHOD: multiply through by the common denominator FIRST, then isolate the requested letter. | TRAP: when the target letter appears twice, you must collect both occurrences before factoring it out. That is the intended difficulty.

column1: 09 ADV-GEO · Similar triangles inside right triangles
column2: An altitude drawn to the hypotenuse creates THREE similar triangles. | Corresponding sides are proportional; set up one ratio and solve. | SIGNAL: 'DE is parallel to BC' or a segment drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse.

column1: 09 ADV-GEO · Area ratios in similar figures
column2: Lengths scale by k, AREAS by k^2, VOLUMES by k^3. | Two similar triangles with sides in a 2:3 ratio have areas in a 4:9 ratio. | The test reliably gives a length ratio and asks for area or volume. Square or cube it.

column1: 09 ADV-GEO · Composite and inscribed solids
column2: METHOD: name each simple solid, compute separately, then add or subtract. | A cylinder with a hemisphere on top is two formulas added. A cube with a cylindrical hole is a subtraction. | Sketch and label before computing anything.

column1: 09 ADV-GEO · Coordinate geometry: proving a shape
column2: To show a PARALLELOGRAM, check both pairs of opposite sides have equal slopes. For a RECTANGLE, add that adjacent slopes multiply to -1. For a RHOMBUS, check all four side lengths are equal. | Use slope and distance formulas systematically rather than by eye.

column1: 09 ADV-GEO · Volume with a changing dimension
column2: SIGNAL: 'the radius is doubled while the height is halved'. | METHOD: write the formula, substitute the new expressions, and simplify the RATIO to the original. | Doubling r and halving h in a cylinder gives 4 x (1/2) = twice the volume.

column1: 10 ADV-DATA · Standard deviation comparisons
column2: You are essentially never asked to compute it, only to COMPARE. More spread means larger SD. | Two data sets can share a mean and differ wildly in SD. | Look at how tightly the values cluster around the center, not at the center itself.

column1: 10 ADV-DATA · Margin of error, in depth
column2: The interval is estimate plus-or-minus the margin. A LARGER SAMPLE narrows it; higher confidence widens it. | Population size is irrelevant. | The conclusion applies only to the population actually sampled, which is the most tested subtlety here.

column1: 10 ADV-DATA · Observational study versus experiment
column2: Only a randomized EXPERIMENT with random ASSIGNMENT can support a causal claim. | An observational study, however large, supports only association. | Scan for the words 'randomly assigned'. Without them, eliminate every choice containing 'causes'.

column1: 10 ADV-DATA · Choosing between regression models
column2: Run each candidate in Desmos and compare R^2; closer to 1 is the better fit. | Also check the residual pattern: a curved pattern means the model family is wrong, not just poorly fitted. | Linear, quadratic and exponential are the only three families the test uses.

column1: 10 ADV-DATA · Weighted averages
column2: METHOD: multiply each value by its weight, add the products, then divide by the total weight. | Two groups of unequal size do NOT give the simple average of their two means. | The unequal-size case is exactly what the test tests.

column1: 10 ADV-DATA · Percentiles and quartiles from a box plot
column2: The box spans Q1 to Q3, the line inside is the MEDIAN, and the whiskers reach the extremes. | IQR = Q3 - Q1 and represents the middle 50 percent. | The median is not necessarily centered in the box; a skewed distribution shifts it.

column1: 11 ADV-DESMOS · Two sliders at once
column2: For questions with two unknown constants, add both sliders and adjust them in turn. | Set one from an obvious constraint (a y-intercept, say), then drag the second until the remaining condition is met. | Far faster than solving a symbolic 2x2 system.

column1: 11 ADV-DESMOS · Restricting a domain to isolate an intersection
column2: Add curly braces: y = f(x){x>0}. | Use this when a curve crosses the line more than once and the question wants a specific branch. | Prevents the classic error of clicking the wrong intersection dot.

column1: 11 ADV-DESMOS · Lists for bulk answer testing
column2: Type L = [2, 5, 7, 11] then an expression in L, and Desmos evaluates all four at once. | Ideal for checking which of four answer choices satisfies an equation. | Faster than a table when you only need one column.

column1: 11 ADV-DESMOS · Regression with a locked parameter
column2: For vertex-form fitting where h and k are known, type y1 ~ a(x1 - h)^2 + k with h and k as fixed numbers. | Desmos then solves for a alone, which is more stable than fitting all three. | Useful for projectile questions that hand you the vertex.

column1: 11 ADV-DESMOS · Solving inequalities graphically
column2: Graph both sides and read the x-interval where one curve lies above the other. | For a system, type each inequality and find the overlap shading. | Then check whether the boundary itself is included: solid means yes, dashed means no.

column1: 11 ADV-DESMOS · Statistics functions worth knowing
column2: mean(L), median(L), stdev(L), total(L), min(L), max(L), quartile(L, 1). | Type the list once and query it repeatedly. | Eliminates arithmetic slips on every data question.

column1: 12 TIMING · How to spend the last five minutes
column2: Do NOT start a new hard question. Instead: verify every gridded-in answer's FORMAT, confirm you answered the quantity asked (x versus x+y), and make sure nothing is blank. | Unanswered questions cost the same as wrong ones, so guess on everything.

column1: 12 TIMING · The gridded-in response rules
column2: No commas, no units, no percent signs. Fractions are fine unreduced. Decimals must fill the available digits rather than being rounded early. | Negative answers are allowed in the student-response section. | A correct value in the wrong format scores zero, so this is free points.

column1: 12 TIMING · When to abandon a question mid-solve
column2: If you have spent ninety seconds and are not clearly within two steps of the answer, stop. | The cost is not the question, it is the two easier questions you will not reach. | Flag it, guess, and move. Revisit only if time remains.

column1: 12 TIMING · Sanity-check every answer against the question
column2: Before bubbling, reread the LAST line of the question. | The three most common careless errors: solving for x when they asked for y, giving area when they asked perimeter, and giving the rate when they asked the total. | This check costs five seconds and saves more points than any technique.

column1: 12 TIMING · Plugging in answer choices is a real method
column2: When the algebra looks long and the choices are numbers, just TEST them. Start with B or C so you learn direction from one try. | DESMOS: put all four in a table and evaluate at once. | This is not cheating; it is often the intended fast path.

column1: 12 TIMING · Picking safe numbers for variable-only questions
column2: When every choice contains letters, substitute concrete values. Use 2, 3, 5 and avoid 0 and 1 because they make different expressions look identical. | Test all four choices with your numbers and eliminate. | If two survive, run a second set of numbers.
